(1) the PEP response to stress is more pronounced during a task that elicits a greater adrenergic effect on the myocardium, while the DBP response is more pronounced during one that elicits a larger adrenergic influence on the vascular system; (2) parental hypertension is associated with higher resting SBP and greater stress-induced cardiovascular responses, while high resting SBP in the absence of parental history is not associated with exaggerated cardiovascular responses to stress.

(a) PEP decreases were more pronounced during a reaction time task that evokes enhanced myocardial adrenergic activation than during a cold pressor test that evokes more enhanced vascular adrenergically-mediated vasoconstriction; and (b) high resting SBP, as determined by physician stethoscopic auscultation, was associated with greater stress-evoked cardiovascular responses, while high resting SBP measured using remote devices was not.
PEP decreases were more pronounced during a reaction time task, which evoked enhanced myocardial activity, than during a cold pressor test, which evoked more enhanced vascular activity.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
PEP decreases during the cold presser test are more indicative of myocardial beta-adrenergic activation than during the pseudo-shock task.

PEP decreases are more pronounced in response to stressors that evoke enhanced sympathetic nervous system activity, and that the PEP is a more sensitive indicator of myocardial response to stress than HR, SBP, or DBP.

cardiovascular responses to the two stressors are differentially affected by the degree of sympathetic stimulation, while high resting SBP is associated with greater cardiovascular responsiveness to the cold presser task but not to the reaction time task.
The main takeaway from our work is that
PEP decreases are not simply a reflection of enhanced cardiac contractility, but rather are more likely a result of increased myocardial adrenergic stimulation.

PEP decreases in response to stressors are not simply a function of the magnitude of the cardiovascular responses, and that PEP decreases can occur in the absence of increases in heart rate and blood pressure.
